documents.title: Telehealth Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Video visit, pt in his kitchen, wife helped with the tablet. Identity verified.
Feels well. Still no alcohol. Taking the fenofibrate without trouble.
Labs 5/11: triglycerides down to 196 from 318. LDL 71. A1c 7.6, better. Kidney and liver fine.
With two MIs behind him I'd like the LDL lower than 70, closer to 55. Discussed going up on atorvastatin to 80 mg. He's fine with it. New Rx sent; told him to stop the 40s and use the 80 once daily.
Call with muscle pain or weakness. Labs and visit in about 4 months.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Primary Care Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Masked visit. Cramping and weak legs, thighs and hips mostly, started roughly two weeks after he went up to atorvastatin 80 (changed 5/13). Hard getting up from a low chair and the cramps cut his walks short. No dark urine, no fever. Still on fenofibrate. He mentions the January cholesterol visit and that he had been feeling fine before the dose change.
Hx: CAD with MI two years ago and in 2014, stent. T2DM, HTN.
O: Vitals in flowsheet. Tender to palpation over the proximal thigh muscles both sides. Strength full but effortful. Exam otherwise unremarkable.
A/P: Statin-associated muscle symptoms, likely made worse by fenofibrate on top of the higher dose.
- Stop atorvastatin 80 and fenofibrate now.
- CK, liver panel, BMP today.
- Plan to retry atorvastatin 40, which he took for years without trouble, once he's back to normal.
Will call with results.

documents.title: Primary Care Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Several weeks of a squeezing tightness mid-chest when he walks the hill on his road or carries things upstairs. Goes away within a few minutes when he stops. None at rest, none at night. Different from his heart attacks, which were sudden and much worse.
Exam: comfortable. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. No edema.
ECG in office: sinus, no acute change.
A/P: Exertional chest tightness in a man with CAD and two prior MIs; sounds like stable angina. Cardiology referral sent urgent. ED for rest pain or anything lasting over 15 minutes, he and his wife both understand. Continue aspirin, metoprolol, atorvastatin.

medications.sig: Dissolve 1 tablet under the tongue as needed for chest pain; sit down first; may repeat every 5 minutes, up to 3

reports.text: Bruce protocol. Exercise stopped for chest tightness typical of his complaint. Horizontal ST-segment depression with symptoms, resolving in recovery. No arrhythmia. Appropriate blood pressure response.
reports.conclusion: Positive for inducible ischemia with reproduction of symptoms.

documents.title: Cardiology consultation
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Outside cardiology group
Date of visit: 12/14/2020
Reason: exertional chest tightness

Mr. Conti, 65, known CAD with MIs in 2014 and 2018 and a stent in 2014, and statin intolerance at high dose this summer, now back on atorvastatin 40. He describes a central squeezing tightness going uphill or up stairs that settles with rest.
Medications: aspirin 81, metoprolol succinate 50, atorvastatin 40, lisinopril 20, metformin 1000 BID, insulin glargine, valproic acid, albuterol PRN.
Allergies: no known drug allergies.
Social: former smoker. No alcohol.
Vitals stable. Exam: regular rhythm, no murmur, lungs clear, no edema.
Stress test today reproduced his usual tightness with ischemic ST changes, recovering promptly.

Impression: stable angina pectoris, chronic CAD. Medical management.
Plan:
1. Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg SL as needed. Sit down before using it, as it can make him lightheaded. Must never be combined with erectile dysfunction pills of the PDE-5 type. He tried a tablet in clinic after the test, with relief within a few minutes.
2. Continue aspirin, metoprolol, atorvastatin, lisinopril.
3. Follow-up in 3 months.

Cardiology

documents.title: nitro question
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Had to use one of the little nitro pills shoveling the end of the driveway. Sat down like they said and it went away in a couple minutes. Is it ok to keep them in the truck in the cold?

documents.title: RE: nitro question
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Glad it worked. Keep them in the original glass bottle and on you, in a coat pocket, rather than in the truck; heat, cold and light weaken them. Replace the bottle once opened per the pharmacy label. Let us or cardiology know if you're needing them more often.

documents.title: Primary Care Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Wife spotted blood on his sock about three weeks ago. He never felt anything there. Feet have been numb and tingly for years, worse lying in bed, sometimes keeps him up. Lately has trouble feeling the gas pedal. No fever.
Exam: afebrile. Right sole under the big-toe ball: shallow open area with thick callus around it, no redness or drainage. Both feet insensate to monofilament. Right foot cooler, pulses hard to feel on that side.
A1c 8.9 today.
A/P: plantar wound right foot in a diabetic with neuropathy, needs specialist eyes this week. Podiatry referral called in, seen Monday. Dry dressing, keep weight off it as best he can, no going barefoot. Sugars are too high; we'll come back to that once the foot is sorted.

conditions.label: Type 2 diabetes mellitus with foot ulcer
conditions.note: right plantar first metatarsal head, 2 cm

documents.title: Podiatry consultation
documents.author: podiatry
documents.body:
Outside podiatry practice
Date of visit: 12/13/2021

Referred by his PCP for a right foot wound. 66-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for about 18 years, neuropathy, CAD with stable angina followed by cardiology. His wife noticed blood on his sock about three weeks ago; no pain. Years of night-time numbness and tingling in both feet; recently hard to feel the gas pedal. No fever, chills or drainage; walking unaffected. No back pain or radiating leg symptoms. No prior amputations. Admits he doesn't look at his feet regularly, hasn't seen podiatry in years, and wears one pair of worn work shoes daily. Quit smoking years ago.
ROS: no vision change, falls, bowel or bladder trouble, hand numbness, weight loss or fatigue.
Meds per patient: metformin, insulin glargine, lisinopril, atorvastatin, aspirin, metoprolol, valproic acid, albuterol.
Allergies: none known.

Exam: afebrile. Right plantar first metatarsal head: 2.0 cm shallow ulcer, clean granular base, hyperkeratotic rim. No erythema, edema or fluctuance. Probe to bone negative. Semmes-Weinstein: protective sensation absent over both plantar surfaces including toes and heels. Vibration decreased at both halluces. Capillary refill delayed. DP and PT diminished on the right.
Most recent A1c 8.9%.
ABI in office: right 0.62, left 1.02.

Assessment: neuropathic diabetic foot ulcer right plantar first MTP region, no clinical infection. Peripheral arterial disease right leg by ABI.
Plan: debrided callus; offloading felt and post-op shoe; daily dressing changes taught. Foot X-ray. Vascular surgery consult given the ABI. Back in 3-4 weeks.

Podiatry

reports.text: Right foot, three views. No fracture or dislocation. No cortical erosion or periosteal reaction at the first metatarsal head. No soft-tissue gas. Joint spaces preserved. Scattered vascular calcification.
